cells.quote: Medical students in the intervention group reported a greater number of actual mental health first aid actions at follow-up (p = .006).

O.outcome_detail: 20-item mental health knowledge true/false quiz score

cells.quote: Participants’ mean knowledge scores at baseline were 11.45 (± 1.21) out of possible maximum score of 20, rising by over three points to 14.72 (± 2.14) at post-course (Z = − 2.94, p = .003, n = 11).
cells.note: Single-arm pre-post result among 11 intervention participants who completed the embedded quiz; the study does not report an explicit knowledge-type classification.

O.outcome_detail: mental health first aid intentions

cells.quote: ITT analysis found no main effect for change in mental health first aid intentions between baseline and follow-up (F(1,53) = 3.67, p = .06), but there was a significant interaction between time and group (F(1,53) = 16.03, p = <.001). Mental health first aid intentions improved in the intervention group (Z = 3.07, p = .002), but not in the control group (p = 0.09).
cells.note: The outcome was assessed six weeks after randomisation using open-ended responses coded against the MHFA ALGEE action plan.

O.outcome_detail: self-rated confidence to help a friend with mental health problems

cells.quote: Confidence to help a friend with mental health problems did increase over time (F(1,51) = 21.22, p = <.001) but the group x time interaction failed to reach significance (F(1,51) = 2.98, p = .09).
cells.note: Intention-to-treat repeated-measures analysis; confidence increased over time in both groups, but the intervention-control difference in change was not statistically significant.

O.outcome_detail: confidence to help a friend with mental health problems

cells.quote: While ITT analysis found no significant Group x Time interaction for confidence to help a friend, the non-ITT analysis did show the intervention improved confidence to help a friend with mental health problems (p < .001), and improved mental health knowledge (p = .003).
cells.note: Non-ITT analysis was restricted to participants who completed baseline and follow-up questionnaires (N = 35).

O.outcome_detail: recognition of the mental health condition in a vignette

result.effect: McNemar p = .125 for control; p = 1.00 for intervention

cells.quote: In both the ITT and non-ITT analyses, there were no pre-post changes in identification of the mental health condition (McNemar’s test p = .125 for control, p = 1.00 for intervention).
cells.note: The study reports no pre-post change in either arm; no direct between-group effect estimate for vignette recognition is reported.

O.outcome_detail: loss to follow-up at six weeks

cells.quote: The intervention group reported significantly greater dropout at follow-up (X2(1) = 5.49, p = .019: see Fig. 1): 14 participants (51.9%) were lost to follow-up, including 3 study withdrawals, compared to only 6 (21.4%) in the control group.
cells.note: The entry reports retention/attrition rather than a learning outcome; the intervention group had worse persistence than the control group.

O.outcome_detail: personal stigma toward mental illness

cells.quote: There was also a significant main effect for stigma over time (F(1,53) = 217.66, p = <.001), and a significant group x time interaction (F(1, 53) = 5.48, p = .023). Stigma fell significantly in the intervention group (Z = 2.30, p = .021) but not in the control group.
cells.note: Intention-to-treat repeated-measures ANOVA; stigma was measured with the seven-item personal stigma subscale of the Depression Stigma Scale. Cohen's d = 0.25 is reported in Table 4.

cells.quote: Further analysis showed an 11% improvement in average knowledge levels between pre- and post-intervention scores with statistically significant differences (P < 0.05) recorded for questions concerning the transmission of the Ebola virus among humans, common symptoms of Ebola fever and whether Ebola fever was preventable.
cells.note: The study used a before-and-after design with the same health workers completing pre- and post-tutorial assessments; 87.7% had heard of EVD before the study, while 12.3% had not.

D.comparison: nurses/midwives, laboratory scientists, and other health workers

O.outcome_detail: Pre-to-post Ebola knowledge-score change by professional category

result.effect: PHC workers: +10.1 points; nurses/midwives: +1.3; laboratory scientists: +0.9; other workers: +5.1.

cells.quote: However, the general upward trend in average between pre- and post-EAT scores was reflected among all professional categories with the greatest change in average score of 10.1 being recorded among PHC workers (Table 4).
cells.note: This is a descriptive subgroup comparison; no statistical test comparing professional categories was reported.

O.outcome_detail: agreement with avoiding handshakes and touching Ebola patients

cells.quote: Positive attitudes, e.g. avoiding handshakes with/touching Ebola patients, avoiding bush meat and avoiding to wash the corpses of diseased patients, were reinforced as indicated by increases between pre- and post-EAT scores from 83 to 92%, 57 to 64% and 67 to 79%, respectively (Table 5).
cells.note: The same 203 health workers completed pre- and post-tutorial assessments. The study reports a descriptive increase but no inferential test, power analysis, or equivalence test for this attitude item.
